Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend who has just started assembling furniture asks for a quick video call because the instructions are confusing.
Situation2: They see a group of teenagers ignoring the no-diving signs near the pool edge.
Story: I was sitting in the staff room, still in my red lifeguard shirt, when my phone buzzed. It was Jamie, my best friend, looking frazzled on video chat. “Hey, can you help? I’m stuck with this bookshelf and the instructions make no sense.” I could hear the frustration in his voice, and I knew he’d been having a rough week. As his friend, I wanted to be there for him, to talk him through it and help him feel less alone. But just as I was about to answer, I glanced out the window and saw a group of teenagers at the pool, laughing and lining up at the edge—right under the big NO DIVING sign. My supervisor had drilled it into us: safety first, always intervene. I felt my stomach twist. Jamie needed me, but so did those kids. I could already hear my supervisor’s voice in my head, warning about the risks. My phone kept buzzing, Jamie’s face waiting for help, while outside, the teens edged closer to danger. I stood frozen, torn between the friend who needed me and the duty I couldn’t ignore.
